title: Validated
statement:
Python Engineer · Metaprogramming: descriptors, `__init_subclass__`, metaclasses

Build Validated

A reusable data descriptor that validates on assignment.

>>> class Order:

... quantity = Validated(int, lambda v: v > 0, "must be positive")

>>> o = Order(); o.quantity = 5; o.quantity

5

Requirements:

- Validated(expected_type, predicate=None, message="invalid value")

- __set_name__ learns the attribute name; store the value in the instance's

__dict__ under a private key so two fields never collide.

- Wrong type -> TypeError("<name> must be <type>"); failing predicate ->

ValueError("<name> <message>").

- Reading before any assignment -> AttributeError("<name> is not set").

- Accessing it on the CLASS (Order.quantity) returns the descriptor itself —

that's what obj is None inside __get__ means.

- It IS a data descriptor (it defines __set__), so it must win over an entry the

user pokes directly into instance.__dict__.

Work through this step

  1. Read the contract and identify its boundary cases.
  2. Run the demonstration to explore the concept.
  3. Edit the module file; focus on this step’s function or class.
  4. Run required checks, then explain one design decision in Notes.
Hint

Start with the smallest example in the contract. Read the named failing test; separate the normal behavior from validation and edge cases. Related helpers share this module workspace.

Module concepts & examples

12 — Metaprogramming: descriptors, __init_subclass__, metaclasses

Code that writes code. Every ORM, every serialisation library, every framework you use is

built out of the four tools below. You need them rarely — but when you need them, nothing

else will do.

Order of preference (reach for the *simplest* thing that works):

1. A plain function or decorator

2. __init_subclass__ / __set_name__

3. A descriptor

4. A class decorator

5. A metaclass ← almost never

In plain English

This module is about code that writes code.

Normally you write a class by typing it out. But a class is just an object, created at

runtime, and you can intercept that creation and change it — or build classes from scratch

with no class statement at all.

Why would anyone want that? Because it's how every framework you've ever used works.

When you write a Django model or a pydantic model and suddenly get validation, database

columns and a nice repr you never wrote — that's this. Somebody wrote code that inspects

your class and fills in the rest.

The two ideas worth having:

- A descriptor is an attribute with a brain. Instead of self.age just storing a

number, it can run your code on every read and write — validating, converting, logging.

That's all @property is, and you can build your own.

- __init_subclass__ lets a base class get notified whenever anyone subclasses it —

which is how plugins register themselves automatically just by existing.

Watch out for: this is the most over-used feature in Python. The rule is at the top of

the module: reach for the *simplest* tool that works, and reach for metaclasses basically

never. Clever code is code your colleagues can't debug at 3am.

1. Descriptors

Any object defining __get__ / __set__ / __delete__, used as a class attribute.

property, classmethod, staticmethod and functions themselves are all descriptors.

class Positive:
    def __set_name__(self, owner, name):      # called at class creation: free name binding
        self._name = f"_{name}"

    def __get__(self, obj, objtype=None):
        if obj is None:
            return self                        # accessed on the CLASS, not an instance
        return getattr(obj, self._name)

    def __set__(self, obj, value):
        if value <= 0:
            raise ValueError(f"{self._name[1:]} must be positive")
        setattr(obj, self._name, value)

class Order:
    quantity = Positive()      # one reusable validator, any number of fields

Data vs non-data descriptor: one with __set__ or __delete__ is a *data* descriptor

and takes precedence over the instance __dict__. Without __set__ (e.g.

cached_property), the instance dict wins — which is exactly how caching-by-overwrite works.

Full attribute lookup order for obj.x:

1. data descriptor on the type

2. obj.__dict__["x"]

3. non-data descriptor / class attribute

4. __getattr__

2. __init_subclass__ — the 90% case

class Plugin:
    registry: dict[str, type] = {}

    def __init_subclass__(cls, /, name: str | None = None, **kwargs):
        super().__init_subclass__(**kwargs)     # always cooperate
        cls.registry[name or cls.__name__.lower()] = cls

class CsvPlugin(Plugin, name="csv"): ...        # class keyword arguments land here

This replaces the majority of metaclasses ever written: auto-registration, subclass

validation, and injecting attributes. It's an implicit classmethod — no @classmethod

needed.

3. Class decorators

def add_repr(cls):
    def __repr__(self):
        fields = ", ".join(f"{k}={v!r}" for k, v in vars(self).items())
        return f"{cls.__name__}({fields})"
    cls.__repr__ = __repr__
    return cls

@dataclass is exactly this: a class decorator that reads __annotations__ and writes

methods with exec. Class decorators compose; metaclasses conflict.

4. Metaclasses

A metaclass is the *type of a class*. type is the default.

class Meta(type):
    def __new__(mcls, name, bases, namespace, **kwargs):
        namespace["created_by"] = "Meta"
        return super().__new__(mcls, name, bases, namespace)

class Thing(metaclass=Meta): ...

Legitimate uses: enforcing invariants across an entire hierarchy at definition time,

controlling __prepare__ (the namespace mapping used during class body execution — how

enum detects duplicate members), customising isinstance via __instancecheck__

(how ABCs work).

The cost: metaclass conflicts in multiple inheritance, opaque tracebacks, and tooling

that can't follow your code. If __init_subclass__ can do it, use that.

> "Metaclasses are deeper magic than 99% of users should ever worry about. If you wonder

> whether you need them, you don't." — Tim Peters

5. Dynamic class and function creation

Klass = type("Klass", (Base,), {"field": 1, "method": lambda self: 42})

types.SimpleNamespace, types.new_class, functools.partial, and closures cover most

"I need to generate this dynamically" cases without any of the above.

6. Introspection toolkit

inspect.signature(f), inspect.getsource(f), inspect.getmembers(obj, predicate)
inspect.isclass / isfunction / iscoroutinefunction / ismethod
vars(obj), dir(obj), type(obj).__mro__, obj.__class__
typing.get_type_hints(f)        # resolves string annotations — use THIS, not __annotations__

typing.get_type_hints is what you want in a framework: with

from __future__ import annotations every annotation is a string, and raw

__annotations__ gives you "int" rather than int.

7. When metaprogramming is the wrong answer

If the result is code where "go to definition" fails, where a reader can't tell which

method runs, or where a typo produces silence instead of an error — you've traded a little

typing for a lot of debugging. Explicit beats clever.

Exercises

exercises_12.py, then pytest 12_metaprogramming.

Further reading

- Descriptor HowTo Guide (optional reading: https://docs.python.org/3/howto/descriptor.html) — read it twice

- PEP 487 — __init_subclass__ and __set_name__ (optional reading: https://peps.python.org/pep-0487/)

Required check source
import pytest

from courselib import impl

m = impl("12")


class TestValidated:
    @pytest.fixture
    def Order(self):
        class Order:
            quantity = m.Validated(int, lambda v: v > 0, "must be positive")
            label = m.Validated(str)

        return Order

    def test_accepts_valid_values(self, Order):
        o = Order()
        o.quantity = 5
        o.label = "widgets"
        assert (o.quantity, o.label) == (5, "widgets")

    def test_type_error(self, Order):
        with pytest.raises(TypeError, match="quantity must be int"):
            Order().quantity = "five"

    def test_predicate_error(self, Order):
        with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="quantity must be positive"):
            Order().quantity = 0

    def test_no_predicate_means_type_only(self, Order):
        o = Order()
        o.label = ""
        assert o.label == ""

    def test_unset_attribute(self, Order):
        with pytest.raises(AttributeError, match="quantity is not set"):
            Order().quantity

    def test_fields_are_independent(self, Order):
        a, b = Order(), Order()
        a.quantity = 1
        b.quantity = 2
        assert (a.quantity, b.quantity) == (1, 2)

    def test_two_descriptors_do_not_collide(self, Order):
        o = Order()
        o.quantity = 7
        o.label = "x"
        assert o.quantity == 7

    def test_class_access_returns_the_descriptor(self, Order):
        assert isinstance(Order.quantity, m.Validated)

    def test_is_a_data_descriptor(self, Order):
        o = Order()
        o.quantity = 5
        o.__dict__["quantity"] = 999  # poking the instance dict directly
        assert o.quantity == 5  # the data descriptor still wins

    def test_delete(self, Order):
        o = Order()
        o.quantity = 5
        del o.quantity
        with pytest.raises(AttributeError):
            o.quantity


class TestRegistry:
    @pytest.fixture(autouse=True)
    def isolated_registry(self):
        saved = dict(m.Registry.registry)
        m.Registry.registry.clear()
        yield
        m.Registry.registry.clear()
        m.Registry.registry.update(saved)

    def test_registers_by_lowercased_name(self):
        class JsonHandler(m.Registry):
            pass

        assert m.Registry.registry["jsonhandler"] is JsonHandler

    def test_explicit_key(self):
        class Csv(m.Registry, key="csv"):
            pass

        assert m.Registry.get("csv") is Csv

    def test_duplicate_key_raises(self):
        class First(m.Registry, key="dup"):
            pass

        with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="dup"):

            class Second(m.Registry, key="dup"):
                pass

    def test_abstract_skips_registration(self):
        class Base(m.Registry, abstract=True):
            pass

        assert m.Registry.registry == {}

    def test_grandchildren_register(self):
        class Base(m.Registry, abstract=True):
            pass

        class Child(Base, key="child"):
            pass

        assert m.Registry.get("child") is Child

    def test_unknown_key_lists_known_ones(self):
        class Csv(m.Registry, key="csv"):
            pass

        with pytest.raises(KeyError) as info:
            m.Registry.get("nope")
        assert "csv" in str(info.value)

    def test_cooperates_with_other_hooks(self):
        seen = []

        class Mixin:
            def __init_subclass__(cls, **kwargs):
                super().__init_subclass__(**kwargs)
                seen.append(cls.__name__)

        class Combined(m.Registry, Mixin, key="combined"):
            pass

        assert seen == ["Combined"]  # our hook called super(), so the mixin's ran too


class TestAutoSlots:
    def test_creates_slots(self):
        @m.auto_slots
        class Point:
            x: int
            y: int

        assert Point.__slots__ == ("x", "y")

    def test_no_instance_dict(self):
        @m.auto_slots
        class Point:
            x: int

        p = Point()
        p.x = 1
        assert not hasattr(p, "__dict__")
        with pytest.raises(AttributeError):
            p.z = 3

    def test_methods_survive(self):
        @m.auto_slots
        class Point:
            x: int

            def double(self):
                return self.x * 2

        p = Point()
        p.x = 21
        assert p.double() == 42

    def test_class_attributes_are_not_slotted(self):
        @m.auto_slots
        class Config:
            name: str
            version: int = 1  # has a value, so it stays a class attribute

        assert Config.__slots__ == ("name",)
        assert Config.version == 1

    def test_preserves_metadata(self):
        @m.auto_slots
        class Documented:
            """My docstring."""

            x: int

        assert Documented.__doc__ == "My docstring."
        assert Documented.__name__ == "Documented"

    def test_no_annotations(self):
        @m.auto_slots
        class Empty:
            pass

        assert Empty.__slots__ == ()


class TestCallLogger:
    def test_logs_calls(self):
        log = []

        @m.call_logger(log)
        class Service:
            def run(self, n):
                return n * 2

        assert Service().run(2) == 4
        assert log == ["run(2)"]

    def test_kwargs_rendering(self):
        log = []

        @m.call_logger(log)
        class Service:
            def run(self, a, b=0):
                return a + b

        Service().run(1, b=2)
        assert log == ["run(1, b=2)"]

    def test_private_methods_are_skipped(self):
        log = []

        @m.call_logger(log)
        class Service:
            def _internal(self):
                return 1

            def __init__(self):
                pass

        Service()._internal()
        assert log == []

    def test_exceptions_pass_through_and_are_logged(self):
        log = []

        @m.call_logger(log)
        class Service:
            def boom(self):
                raise ValueError

        with pytest.raises(ValueError):
            Service().boom()
        assert log == ["boom()"]

    def test_metadata_preserved(self):
        log = []

        @m.call_logger(log)
        class Service:
            def documented(self):
                """Docs."""

        assert Service.documented.__name__ == "documented"
        assert Service.documented.__doc__ == "Docs."

    def test_each_method_logs_its_own_name(self):
        log = []

        @m.call_logger(log)
        class Service:
            def a(self):
                pass

            def b(self):
                pass

        s = Service()
        s.a()
        s.b()
        assert log == ["a()", "b()"]  # not ["b()", "b()"] — watch out for late binding


class TestBuildModel:
    @pytest.fixture
    def User(self):
        return m.build_model("User", {"id": int, "name": str})

    def test_construction_and_attributes(self, User):
        u = User(id=1, name="ada")
        assert (u.id, u.name) == (1, "ada")

    def test_repr(self, User):
        assert repr(User(id=1, name="ada")) == "User(id=1, name='ada')"

    def test_class_name(self, User):
        assert User.__name__ == "User"

    def test_keyword_only(self, User):
        with pytest.raises(TypeError):
            User(1, "ada")

    def test_missing_field(self, User):
        with pytest.raises(TypeError, match="name"):
            User(id=1)

    def test_unknown_field(self, User):
        with pytest.raises(TypeError, match="admin"):
            User(id=1, name="a", admin=True)

    def test_type_validation(self, User):
        with pytest.raises(TypeError, match="id must be int"):
            User(id="one", name="ada")

    def test_equality_by_value(self, User):
        assert User(id=1, name="a") == User(id=1, name="a")
        assert User(id=1, name="a") != User(id=2, name="a")

    def test_different_models_are_not_equal(self, User):
        Other = m.build_model("User", {"id": int, "name": str})
        assert User(id=1, name="a") != Other(id=1, name="a")

    def test_hashable(self, User):
        assert len({User(id=1, name="a"), User(id=1, name="a")}) == 1

    def test_metadata(self, User):
        assert User.__annotations__ == {"id": int, "name": str}
        assert User._fields == ("id", "name")

    def test_independent_models(self):
        A = m.build_model("A", {"x": int})
        B = m.build_model("B", {"y": str})
        assert A(x=1).x == 1
        assert B(y="s").y == "s"

"""Module 12 exercises.  pytest 12_metaprogramming

Build the machinery frameworks are made of. Annotate everything — mypy runs strict on
this file.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from collections.abc import Callable
from typing import Any


class Validated:
    """A reusable data descriptor that validates on assignment.

    >>> class Order:
    ...     quantity = Validated(int, lambda v: v > 0, "must be positive")
    >>> o = Order(); o.quantity = 5; o.quantity
    5

    Requirements:
    - `Validated(expected_type, predicate=None, message="invalid value")`
    - `__set_name__` learns the attribute name; store the value in the instance's
      `__dict__` under a private key so two fields never collide.
    - Wrong type -> TypeError("<name> must be <type>"); failing predicate ->
      ValueError("<name> <message>").
    - Reading before any assignment -> AttributeError("<name> is not set").
    - Accessing it on the CLASS (`Order.quantity`) returns the descriptor itself —
      that's what `obj is None` inside `__get__` means.
    - It IS a data descriptor (it defines `__set__`), so it must win over an entry the
      user pokes directly into `instance.__dict__`.
    """

    def __init__(
        self,
        expected_type: type,
        predicate: Callable[[Any], bool] | None = None,
        message: str = "invalid value",
    ) -> None:
        raise NotImplementedError


class Registry:
    """A base class whose subclasses register themselves automatically.

    >>> class Handler(Registry): pass          # doctest: +SKIP
    >>> class Json(Handler, key="json"): pass  # doctest: +SKIP
    >>> Handler.registry["json"] is Json       # doctest: +SKIP
    True

    Requirements, all via `__init_subclass__` (no metaclass):
    - Subclasses register under the `key=` class keyword argument, defaulting to the
      lowercased class name.
    - `Registry.registry` is a dict[str, type].
    - Registering a duplicate key raises ValueError at class-definition time.
    - `abstract=True` as a class keyword skips registration (for intermediate bases).
    - Always call `super().__init_subclass__(**kwargs)` so the hook composes with others.
    - `Registry.get(key)` returns the class, raising KeyError with a message listing the
      known keys.
    """

    registry: dict[str, type] = {}


def auto_slots(cls: type) -> type:
    """A CLASS DECORATOR that rebuilds `cls` with `__slots__` from its annotations.

    >>> @auto_slots                       # doctest: +SKIP
    ... class Point:
    ...     x: int
    ...     y: int

    - The returned class must have `__slots__ == ("x", "y")` and no `__dict__`.
    - You cannot add `__slots__` to an existing class — the layout is fixed at creation.
      Rebuild it with `type(cls.__name__, cls.__bases__, namespace)`, copying the
      original namespace, dropping `__dict__`/`__weakref__`, and adding `__slots__`.
    - Class-level attributes that have a VALUE (defaults, methods) must be excluded from
      `__slots__` — a slot and a class attribute of the same name conflict.
    - Preserve `__doc__`, `__module__`, and `__qualname__`.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError


def call_logger(sink: list[str]) -> Callable[[type], type]:
    """A class-decorator FACTORY that logs every public method call into `sink`.

    >>> log = []                                   # doctest: +SKIP
    >>> @call_logger(log)                          # doctest: +SKIP
    ... class Service:
    ...     def run(self, n): return n * 2
    >>> Service().run(2); log                      # doctest: +SKIP
    (4, ['run(2)'])

    - Wrap every callable attribute whose name doesn't start with "_".
    - Log entries are "<name>(<comma-separated reprs of args and kwargs>)", where `self`
      is not included and kwargs are rendered as "k=v" after the positional args.
    - Return values and exceptions pass through untouched (log the call either way).
    - Use `functools.wraps`; `staticmethod` and `classmethod` may be left alone.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError


def build_model(name: str, fields: dict[str, type]) -> type:
    """Create a class at runtime from a field spec — a miniature ORM model factory.

    >>> User = build_model("User", {"id": int, "name": str})   # doctest: +SKIP
    >>> u = User(id=1, name="ada"); repr(u)                    # doctest: +SKIP
    "User(id=1, name='ada')"

    The generated class must:
    - Take all fields as KEYWORD-ONLY arguments; a missing one raises TypeError,
      an unknown one raises TypeError.
    - Validate types on construction: wrong type raises TypeError.
    - Provide `__repr__` as "Name(field=value, ...)" in declaration order.
    - Compare by value (`==`) against other instances of the same generated class, and
      be hashable.
    - Expose `__annotations__` equal to `fields`, and a `_fields` tuple of names.

    Use `type(name, bases, namespace)`. This is the exercise where you feel why
    `@dataclass` exists.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError
